name: Spironolactone for hormonal acne

card.summary: A prescription anti-androgen that dermatologists prescribe to some adult women with hormonal acne to reduce oil production and breakouts, clearing the skin over a few months.
card.note: Prescription-only; potassium effects, menstrual changes and pregnancy considerations apply, and it is generally not used for acne in men.

quick.overview:
Spironolactone is a prescription medicine that blocks aldosterone and, to a lesser degree, androgens. Doctors use it off the main label for acne in adult women, especially breakouts along the jaw and chin linked to hormones, as an alternative to long courses of antibiotics.

The appearance payoff is clearer, less oily skin. It reduces the skin's oil production, and results are described as taking one to three months. Randomized trials, including a large phase 3 study in adult women and a comparison with doxycycline, have been registered to test it.
quick.how: It is prescribed by a doctor, taken by mouth, and often combined with a birth control pill or topical treatments. Follow-up typically covers blood pressure and, in some cases, potassium. Users on forums mention being prescribed it for acne, including men on testosterone therapy asking whether it fits their regimen.
quick.risks: Reported effects include high potassium (rarely serious in healthy young women), menstrual irregularity, breast tenderness, nausea, headache, dizziness and increased urination. It is not recommended in pregnancy because of possible effects on a male fetus. It is contraindicated with high potassium, severe kidney disease, Addison's disease and eplerenone, and its feminizing effects mean it is generally not used for acne in men.

lead: Spironolactone is a prescription medicine first introduced in 1959 as a diuretic that blocks the hormone aldosterone and, to a lesser degree, testosterone.[4] The acne benefit was discovered as a side effect, and it is now used as a possible alternative to antibiotics for hormonal acne in adult women, often alongside a contraceptive pill.[4]

People use it for appearance because it reduces skin oil production and, over roughly one to three months, can reduce inflammatory breakouts.[4] Because it is an anti-androgen, it is aimed at acne driven by hormones rather than at all acne.

Several registered trials examine it: a phase 3 randomized double-blind study in adult women with acne,[2] a phase 4 comparative effectiveness trial against doxycycline,[1] and a planned split-face study of a 5% topical gel against adapalene.[3] Discussion in forums such as T Nation includes people mentioning prescriptions and topical anti-androgen ideas for acne.[5][6]

chain: Blocks androgen action on the skin
Fewer clogged pores and inflamed spots
Clearer skin after one to three months
angle.text: Prescribed to adult women with hormonal acne, spironolactone lowers the androgen-driven oil production behind jawline breakouts. It is often paired with a contraceptive pill or a topical.

paras: For acne, spironolactone is used mainly in adult women whose breakouts have a hormonal pattern. Wikipedia notes it is considered a possible alternative to antibiotics, with modest benefit in recent trials but limited short-term outcome data.[4] It is often combined with an oral contraceptive.[4]
Men are generally not treated with it for androgen-dependent skin conditions because of feminizing effects, and the high doses needed for anti-androgen action are not recommended for men.[4]
It is a steroid that blocks aldosterone and, less strongly, androgen receptors, which reduces the oil the skin produces.[4]

Hyperkalemia is the best-known concern, though a 2017 review found it rare and mild in young healthy women without kidney or heart disease.[4] Menstrual irregularities were reported in about 13.4 percent of randomized-trial participants and 33.4 percent in case series, more so at higher doses; breast tenderness or enlargement, nausea, headache and dizziness are also reported.[4] Animal studies suggest effects on male fetal sex-organ development, so pregnancy needs discussion with a doctor.[4]

A T Nation thread records a user prescribed 25 mg daily for acne asking about use alongside testosterone therapy,[6] and another thread mentions spironolactone cream as a topical anti-androgen people had heard of for back acne.[5]

Registered trials include NCT03334682, a phase 3 randomized double-blind study in 158 adult women with acne vulgaris that began in 2018 and has completed;[2] NCT04582383, a phase 4 trial of 350 participants comparing spironolactone with doxycycline, active as of its listing;[1] and NCT07473895, a planned split-face trial of 5% spironolactone gel against 0.1% adapalene gel in 40 participants.[3]

timeline.event: Phase 3 trial in adult women with acne begins.[2]
